questions.question: Q: What does FATTOM stand for?

points.text: Food, Acidity, Temperature, Time, Oxygen, Moisture — the six conditions microorganisms need to grow.

questions.question: Q: What is the danger zone temperature range for bacterial growth?

points.text: 5°C to 63°C. Bacteria multiply fastest at around 37°C (body temperature).

questions.question: Q: Name three signs of food spoilage.

points.text: Unpleasant smell, discolouration, slime, visible mould, gas bubbles, or off-taste (any three).

questions.question: Q: How does pasteurisation help prevent spoilage?

points.text: It heats food to 72°C for 15 seconds, killing most harmful bacteria without significantly changing the food's flavour or nutritional value.

questions.question: Q: Why does freezing at −18°C not kill bacteria?

points.text: Freezing stops bacterial growth by making water unavailable, but bacteria survive in a dormant state and can reactivate when the food is thawed.

questions.question: Q: What is the difference between food spoilage and food poisoning?

points.text: Spoilage makes food unpalatable (bad smell, taste, appearance) but may not always cause illness. Food poisoning is caused by consuming harmful bacteria or their toxins and causes illness.

questions.question: Q: How do yeasts cause spoilage?

points.text: Yeasts ferment sugars, producing alcohol and carbon dioxide gas. This causes food to smell yeasty, taste sour, or develop gas bubbles.

questions.question: Q: What are mycotoxins and which microorganism produces them?

points.text: Mycotoxins are harmful chemical substances produced by moulds. They can cause illness even if the mould is removed.
